g.text: Window shapes — fixed, sliding, and session
fixed 4 windows totalling 45 · sliding totals 78 · sessions 4/3/2/1 for key a as the gap grows
FIXED (TUMBLING) — 120s EACH, NO OVERLAP, NO GAPS
every one of the 9 events is in exactly one row
The sums total 45, which is the whole dataset — because the windows partition event time.
This is the shape that reconciles against a batch job: "how many per 120s" has one answer per period and no double counting.
Step 1/4 — fixed windows partition time: one event, one window
Fixed windows are the easy case and the one to reach for by default. Equal length, contiguous, non-overlapping — so each of the 9 events appears
exactly once and the 4 sums add to 45. If a question names a period ("per minute", "per hour"), this is the shape, and nothing else needs
Window shapes — fixed, sliding, and session
fixed 4 windows totalling 45 · sliding totals 78 · sessions 4/3/2/1 for key a as the gap grows
how many windows each event belongs to, under each shape
6 of the 9 events land in 2 windows at once, so the sliding results total 78 against the dataset's 45.
Output volume scales with WIN / PERIOD = 120 / 60 = 2x. That is the cost of a smooth moving measure.
Step 2/4 — sliding windows overlap: one event, several windows
Sliding windows answer "the rolling 120s figure, refreshed every 60s". Read the third column: 6 events are in 2 windows, which is why the totals
cannot be compared to the input. The first few events are in one window only because event time starts at 12:00 — there is no window before it.
Window shapes — fixed, sliding, and session
fixed 4 windows totalling 45 · sliding totals 78 · sessions 4/3/2/1 for key a as the gap grows
SESSIONS — A BURST, SEPARATED BY 120s OF SILENCE
key a gets 3 sessions, key b gets 2 — from the same stream
No session has the same length as any other, and none starts on a round boundary. Both facts follow from the boundaries being set by the DATA.
Key a gets 3 and key b gets 2 over the same 540s of event time, because they were active at different moments.
Step 3/4 — session windows are defined by the DATA, not the clock
Sessions model behaviour rather than counting. Every boundary here was chosen by a silence of more than 120s: key a's first session ends at
12:00:03 because its next activity is 127s later. That is why two users over one time span get 3 and 2 sessions, not the same number.
Window shapes — fixed, sliding, and session
fixed 4 windows totalling 45 · sliding totals 78 · sessions 4/3/2/1 for key a as the gap grows
THE SAME STREAM, FOUR GAP SETTINGS
session count per key, as the gap grows
Key a goes 4 → 3 → 2 → 1 sessions as the gap grows. The events never change; only the definition of "a visit" does.
So "how many sessions did this user have?" has no answer until someone states the gap. It is a product definition that happens to be typed into a
Step 4/4 — and the gap is part of the ANSWER, not a tuning knob
This is the step that matters most in practice. Key a has 4, 3, 2, 1 sessions at gaps of 40s, 120s, 130s, 300s — four different answers from
identical data. The gap is not a performance setting; it is the operational definition of "a visit", and choosing it is the product decision the
